newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican evacuees say blast district a time bomb.
newsitem.headline: Mexican evacuees say blast district a time bomb.

text.p: Evacuees from the huge gasoline storage tank blast that killed one person and injured at least 14 said on Tuesday they had lived for years in fear atop a "ticking time bomb."

Twelve years ago, an explosion at a liquefied petroleum gas facility here killed at least 511 people, sending a tongue of flame ripping through ramshackle homes, many made of cardboard, and leaving hundreds more crippled for life.
"It is a time bomb waiting to explode," one elderly housewife said as she waited in line for the lavatories at one of the shelters set up for more than 5,000 evacuees.
Years of complaints to the state oil monopoly Pemex and the government about repeated fires and gas leaks had fallen on deaf ears, residents said.

"All the area neighbours have asked Pemex to remove the gas tanks from the region...but they don't listen," said Josefina Pastrana Lozano, former area mayoress for the opposition National Action Party.
Watching the black mushroom cloud of smoke shooting into the air in Monday's explosion, Pastrana recalled nudging her husband and saying: "Look, they've done it again."

Black smoke continued to billow from the devastated tanks on Tuesday, 24 hours after the original blast, but many of the residents taken from the area say they will have to return anyway because they fear their homes are being pillaged.
"People are concerned because their houses are not well protected and there are many thieves there," said 22-year-old housewife Aurora Flores, huddled in a blanket on the floor.
"For the last 12 years that we have been complaining, they have preferred to relocate us rather than the tanks."
"Pemex has all the millions in the world to remove these tanks...and we have been waiting, but unfortunately they have done nothing," Pastrana said.
Some residents near the oil and gas monopoly's facility in San Juan have resigned themselves to their grim lives.
"The explosion shook the house, but we already knew what it was because of the last time," said a 31-year-old housewife, who would not give her name.
According to women discussing the issue at an emergency shelter, any move would be too expensive to afford.

"Humble people live in this area. If they had money, believe me, they would not be living here. In reality, we are not going to move because we haven't the money or anywhere to go," said a 64-year-old who also asked to remain anonymous.
